questions.stem: You can hear someone talking around a corner, but you cannot see them. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Sound waves reflect off the walls better than light
Sound waves have a much longer wavelength than light, so they diffract more around the corner
Sound waves travel faster than light around corners

questions.explanation: Diffraction is most significant when the wavelength is similar to or larger than the size of the gap or obstacle. Sound waves have wavelengths of roughly 0.02 m to 17 m, comparable to a doorway, so they diffract well around corners. Visible light has wavelengths around 400-700 nm — far too small compared to a doorway to show noticeable diffraction. Option D is wrong — light can diffract, but the effect is only noticeable with very small gaps.

questions.stem: In a ripple tank, a wave with a wavelength of 2 cm approaches a gap. For which gap width would the most noticeable diffraction occur?
questions.explanation: Maximum diffraction occurs when the gap width is approximately equal to the wavelength of the wave. With a 2 cm wavelength, a 2 cm gap gives the greatest spreading. Gaps much smaller than the wavelength (0.2 cm) would block most of the wave. Gaps much larger (20 cm, 200 cm) would allow the wave through with very little spreading.

questions.stem: A harbour has a narrow entrance. Long-wavelength ocean waves spread out as they pass through the entrance, but short-wavelength ripples do not. This is because:

options.text: Short-wavelength waves are reflected by the harbour walls
The entrance width is comparable to the long wavelength but much larger than the short wavelength

questions.explanation: Diffraction depends on the ratio of wavelength to gap size. When the gap width is similar to the wavelength, significant diffraction (spreading) occurs. The harbour entrance is comparable in size to long ocean waves, causing them to spread, but is much larger than short ripples, which pass through with little spreading. Energy (A) and speed (D) are not the determining factors for diffraction.

questions.stem: Radio waves with a wavelength of 300 m can diffract around hills, but FM radio waves with a wavelength of 3 m cannot diffract as effectively around the same hills. A hill is approximately 100 m wide. What does this tell us about diffraction?

options.text: Waves diffract more when their wavelength is comparable to or larger than the obstacle
FM waves are too fast to diffract
FM waves are absorbed by the hill material

questions.explanation: The 300 m wavelength is larger than the 100 m hill, so significant diffraction occurs and the wave bends around the hill. The 3 m FM wavelength is much smaller than the hill, so diffraction is minimal and a 'shadow' forms behind it. Option A is wrong — all waves can diffract; the extent depends on the wavelength-to-obstacle ratio. Speed (option C) does not determine diffraction ability.

questions.stem: A student shines a laser through a very narrow single slit. They observe a broad central bright band on the screen with dimmer bands on either side. If the slit is made narrower, what happens to the central bright band?

options.text: It stays the same width but gets brighter

questions.explanation: A narrower slit means the gap width is closer to the wavelength of light, causing more diffraction and greater spreading. This makes the central bright band wider (but dimmer, as the same energy is spread over a larger area). Option A is a common misconception — students often think a smaller gap produces a smaller pattern, but the opposite is true for diffraction.
